title: Plasma Protein Patterns: Acute Phase, α1-Antitrypsin and the Haptoglobin Clue
summary: Read SPEP zone patterns for α1-antitrypsin deficiency, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and inflammation; use CRP and the negative acute-phase proteins; and separate hemoglobinuria from myoglobinuria with haptoglobin, LD and CK, knowing haptoglobin’s blind spots.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 20 Hits 3–6, 11 and 12 and Traps 2, 3 and 5. Checked against O’Connell 2005, Jain 2011, Sproston & Ashworth 2018, Abboud 2011, Barcellini & Fattizzo 2015, Smith & McCulloh 2015, Kapatia 2021, Chhabra 2013, Petejova & Martinek 2014 and Gupta 2021. Hit 4 says myoglobin does not bind haptoglobin, but two rhabdomyolysis reviews say circulating myoglobin is bound mainly by haptoglobin (register flag rv-myoglobin-hp); the lesson separates the two by CK instead. Trap 2 omits acquired bisalbuminemia (register flag rv-bisalbumin). Not taught: α2-macroglobulin 725 kDa and its 10-fold rise, δ-bilirubin speeding albumin (Trap 4), “very high CRP favors bacterial over viral,” haptoglobin “rebounds quickly” and hemopexin staying low longer, ZZ prevalence 1 in 4000.

objectives: Name the main proteins in each SPEP zone and classify positive and negative acute-phase proteins.
Recognize SPEP patterns of α1-antitrypsin deficiency, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, inflammation and iron deficiency.
Separate hemoglobinuria from myoglobinuria using haptoglobin, LD and CK.
Explain why a normal haptoglobin does not exclude hemolysis and recognize benign and acquired bisalbuminemia.

scenes.title: Same strip, different pigment
scenes.altText: Two patient cards side by side, both with dark urine: dipstick blood 3+, microscopy 0–2 RBC/hpf. Patient A: haptoglobin < 10 mg/dL, LD high, CK normal. Patient B (crush injury): haptoglobin normal, CK 48,000 U/L. A question token: “Same strip — which pigment is which?” The cartoon scientist squints at the strips.

cues.text: Two patients, both with dark urine. Both dipsticks are strongly positive for blood, yet the microscope shows almost no red cells.
Patient A has an undetectable haptoglobin and a high LD. Patient B was crushed under a beam: haptoglobin normal, creatine kinase 48,000.
Same strip, different pigment. Plasma proteins tell you which, if you know what each one does.

props.label: Same strip — which pigment is which?

scenes.title: Five zones, and the acute-phase response
scenes.altText: A schematic SPEP lane with five zones labelled by the proteins they carry: α1 (α1-antitrypsin), α2 (haptoglobin, α2-macroglobulin, ceruloplasmin), β (transferrin, β-lipoprotein, complement), γ (immunoglobulins), with albumin leading. An inflammation spark appears: up-arrows on CRP, α1-antitrypsin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin, complement (positive acute-phase proteins); down-arrows on albumin, transferrin, transthyretin (negative). A CRP gauge jumps up to ×1000 then decays with a ~19-hour half-life.

cues.text: Most plasma proteins are made in the liver, and each lands in its own zone on electrophoresis. Alpha-1 is mostly alpha-1-antitrypsin.
Alpha-2 holds haptoglobin, alpha-2-macroglobulin and ceruloplasmin. Beta holds transferrin, beta-lipoprotein and complement. Gamma holds the immunoglobulins.
Inflammation reprograms the liver. Positive acute-phase proteins rise: CRP, alpha-1-antitrypsin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin and complement.
Negative acute-phase proteins fall: albumin, transferrin and transthyretin, also called prealbumin.
CRP is the sprinter. Some bacterial infections raise it up to a thousandfold, and once the stimulus stops it falls with a half-life of about 19 hours, so it tracks inflammation closely.

props.label: ↑ CRP · AAT · Hp · fibrinogen · Cp · C3

keys.label: CRP t½ ≈ 19 h after stimulus ends

scenes.title: Patterns that point to a disease
scenes.altText: Four mini-lanes appear, each with the changed zone highlighted. α1-antitrypsin deficiency: α1 band absent or faint (ZZ ≈ 15% of normal) → early emphysema, worse in smokers; retained Z protein injures the liver. Nephrotic syndrome: albumin low, α2 raised. Cirrhosis: albumin low, broad polyclonal γ rise. Iron deficiency: β (transferrin) band raised — not an M-spike; immunofixation settles doubt. An inflammation lane: α1 and α2 up, albumin down.

cues.text: A missing alpha-1 band is the classic picture of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency. ZZ homozygotes have about 15 percent of normal levels, so the band is absent or faint.
Without its main inhibitor, neutrophil elastase destroys lung elastin, causing emphysema at a young age, especially in smokers. The trapped Z protein also injures the liver.
Nephrotic syndrome leaks albumin into the urine, so albumin falls while the alpha-2 band rises.
Cirrhosis lowers albumin, because the liver makes less, and raises gamma as a broad, polyclonal hump, not a narrow spike.

Iron deficiency raises transferrin, so the beta band grows. A narrow beta band can look like a monoclonal spike; immunofixation settles it. And acute inflammation raises alpha-1 and alpha-2 while albumin drops.

scenes.title: Haptoglobin: the hemoglobin scavenger, and its blind spots
scenes.altText: A flow: urine dipstick heme+ with no RBCs → “free hemoglobin or myoglobin.” Branch 1 (hemolysis): haptoglobin (an α2 protein) binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → haptoglobin falls; LD rises; hemosiderinuria later in marked intravascular hemolysis. Branch 2 (rhabdomyolysis): CK markedly raised. A caveat card: haptoglobin is a positive acute-phase protein — inflammation, smoking and nephrotic syndrome raise it and can mask hemolysis; liver disease, malnutrition and congenital hypohaptoglobinemia lower it without hemolysis. Hemopexin binds free heme and is not an acute-phase protein in humans. Back to the hook: A = hemolysis (hemoglobinuria); B = rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria).

cues.text: A blood-positive dipstick with no red cells means free pigment: hemoglobin or myoglobin. The strip reacts with both.
In hemolysis, haptoglobin binds the free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared, so haptoglobin falls and LD rises. Marked intravascular hemolysis later adds hemosiderin to the urine.
In rhabdomyolysis, the giveaway is a very high creatine kinase.
Haptoglobin has blind spots. It is an acute-phase protein, so inflammation, smoking and nephrotic syndrome raise it and can hide hemolysis. Liver disease and malnutrition lower it without hemolysis.
Hemopexin, which binds free heme, is not an acute-phase protein in humans. So patient A has hemolysis with hemoglobinuria; patient B has rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria.

props.label: Heme+ dipstick, no RBCs → free Hb or myoglobin

props.title: Haptoglobin blind spots
lines: ↓ without hemolysis: liver disease · malnutrition · congenital

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Dipstick blood + no RBCs = hematuria” (✓ free hemoglobin or myoglobin — check haptoglobin, LD, CK); “Normal haptoglobin rules out hemolysis” (✓ not during inflammation — haptoglobin is acute-phase; use LD, reticulocytes, bilirubin, smear); “Two albumin bands = liver disease work-up” (✓ bisalbuminemia: hereditary form permanent and benign; acquired form transient — high-dose β-lactams, pancreatic pseudocyst).

cues.text: Trap one: dipstick positive for blood with no red cells means hematuria. No. It is free hemoglobin or myoglobin. Check haptoglobin, LD and CK.
Trap two: a normal haptoglobin rules out hemolysis. Not in an inflamed patient, because haptoglobin rises in the acute phase. Lean on LD, reticulocytes, bilirubin and the smear.
Trap three: two albumin bands mean liver disease. Hereditary bisalbuminemia is permanent and benign. An acquired, transient form follows high-dose beta-lactams or a pancreatic pseudocyst.

props.title: ✗ “Dipstick blood + no RBCs = hematuria.”

props.title: ✗ “Normal haptoglobin rules out hemolysis.”

scenes.title: The haptoglobin sponge
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Haptoglobin is a sponge: it soaks up free hemoglobin and empties in hemolysis — but inflammation makes the sponge bigger.” A sponge token shrinks (hemolysis) and swells (inflammation). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: haptoglobin is a sponge. It soaks up free hemoglobin and runs dry in hemolysis. But inflammation makes the sponge bigger.
Where it breaks: the sponge is cleared together with its load, not wrung out; liver disease shrinks it without hemolysis; and myoglobinuria is diagnosed with CK, not with the sponge.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: The Hb–Hp complex is cleared, not wrung out
Liver disease shrinks it without hemolysis

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Absent α1 = AAT deficiency · nephrotic: albumin ↓ α2 ↑ · cirrhosis: albumin ↓ polyclonal γ ↑ · CRP fast up, fast down”, “Heme+ no RBCs: low Hp + LD ↑ = hemolysis · CK ↑↑ = rhabdo · Hp is acute-phase”.

cues.text: Read SPEP zones for patterns, use CRP to follow inflammation, and remember that haptoglobin falls in hemolysis but rises with inflammation.

props.label: No α1 = AAT deficiency · nephrotic: Alb ↓ α2 ↑ · cirrhosis: Alb ↓ polyclonal γ ↑
Heme+, no RBCs: Hp ↓ + LD ↑ = hemolysis · CK ↑↑ = rhabdo · Hp is acute-phase

explanation.what: Plain language: the liver makes most plasma proteins; their levels shift in predictable ways in inflammation, liver and kidney disease, and hemolysis. Scientific terms: α1-antitrypsin (AAT, SERPINA1, Pi ZZ), haptoglobin (Hp), hemopexin (HPX), α2-macroglobulin, C-reactive protein (CRP), positive and negative acute-phase proteins, polyclonal gammopathy, bisalbuminemia.
explanation.why: IL-6–driven acute-phase response raises CRP, AAT, Hp, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin and complement and lowers albumin, transferrin and transthyretin. AAT is the main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase; the Z variant polymerizes and is retained in hepatocytes. Hp binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared, so Hp falls in hemolysis. Cirrhosis lowers albumin synthesis and raises polyclonal immunoglobulins.
explanation.measure: CRP: up to ~1000-fold rise in some bacterial infections; falls with a half-life of ~18–20 h after the stimulus ends. ZZ AAT ≈ 15% of normal; diagnosis by AAT level (immunoassay), phenotype (isoelectric focusing) and genotyping. Hemolysis markers: low Hp, high LD, reticulocytosis, unconjugated bilirubin; hemosiderinuria in marked intravascular hemolysis. Rhabdomyolysis: markedly raised CK.
explanation.differs: Hemoglobinuria (low Hp, high LD) vs myoglobinuria (very high CK). Polyclonal γ (broad, cirrhosis or inflammation) vs monoclonal spike (narrow). Hereditary bisalbuminemia (permanent, benign) vs acquired (transient, faster band; high-dose β-lactams, pancreatic pseudocyst). Transferrin β band in iron deficiency vs paraprotein (immunofixation).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: absent α1 band and emphysema, nephrotic and cirrhosis patterns, CRP for monitoring, albumin as a negative acute-phase protein, heme-positive dipstick without RBCs, haptoglobin masked by inflammation, and bisalbuminemia.

comparisons.title: Hemoglobinuria vs myoglobinuria
comparisons.distinguisher: Both give a heme-positive dipstick without RBCs; haptoglobin/LD vs CK separates them.

comparisons.title: Nephrotic syndrome vs cirrhosis on SPEP
comparisons.distinguisher: Which globulin zone rises: α2 in nephrotic syndrome, γ in cirrhosis.

mnemonic.explanation: It soaks up free hemoglobin and runs dry in hemolysis, but inflammation makes the sponge bigger.
mnemonic.limitation: The Hb–Hp complex is cleared, not wrung out; liver disease shrinks haptoglobin without hemolysis; myoglobinuria is diagnosed with CK, not haptoglobin.

The patients and values are invented.
The sponge analogy ignores clearance kinetics and CD163-mediated uptake.

questions.stem: After a crush injury, a patient has dark urine, dipstick blood 3+, 0–2 RBC/hpf, normal haptoglobin and CK 48,000 U/L. What is the most likely urine pigment?

options.rationale: Correct. A heme-positive strip without RBCs plus a very high CK points to myoglobinuria.
Incorrect. Hemolysis would typically lower haptoglobin; the very high CK points to muscle.

options.text: Red cells lysed in the bladder (hematuria)
options.rationale: Incorrect. Microscopy shows almost no RBCs, and the clinical picture fits muscle injury.
Incorrect. Bilirubin does not make the blood pad positive.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old smoker with early emphysema has an SPEP in which the α1 band is barely visible. What is the best next laboratory step?

options.text: Measure serum α1-antitrypsin and determine the phenotype or genotype
options.rationale: Correct. A faint α1 band suggests AAT deficiency; AAT is quantified by immunoassay and characterized by isoelectric focusing and genotyping.

options.text: Serum immunofixation for a monoclonal protein
options.rationale: Incorrect. The abnormality is a missing α1 band, not an extra spike.
Incorrect. Haptoglobin sits in α2 and does not explain a missing α1 band.

options.text: Repeat in plasma instead of serum
options.rationale: Incorrect. Plasma adds fibrinogen; it does not restore α1.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia (CRP 180 mg/L) has falling hemoglobin, a raised LD and reticulocytes, but a normal haptoglobin. How should the haptoglobin be interpreted?

options.text: It does not exclude hemolysis; haptoglobin is an acute-phase protein that inflammation can raise
options.rationale: Correct. Inflammation can mask the haptoglobin drop; rely on LD, reticulocytes, bilirubin and the smear.
Incorrect. A normal haptoglobin during inflammation can hide hemolysis.
Incorrect. Liver disease lowers haptoglobin; it does not explain a normal value.

options.text: It means the CRP is falsely high
options.rationale: Incorrect. CRP and haptoglobin both rise in the acute phase; neither falsifies the other.

references.citation: O’Connell TX, Horita TJ, Kasravi B. Understanding and interpreting serum protein electrophoresis. Am Fam Physician. 2005;71(1):105-112.
references.usedFor: Zone contents; decreased α1 band in AAT deficiency; α2 increased as acute-phase reactant; acute-reaction pattern (fibrinogen, AAT, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, CRP, C3 up; albumin and transferrin down); decreased albumin in nephrotic syndrome and liver disease; increased α2 in nephrotic syndrome; increased β in iron deficiency anemia; increased γ in cirrhosis; polyclonal gammopathies from reactive processes.

references.citation: Jain S, Gautam V, Naseem S. Acute-phase proteins: as diagnostic tool. J Pharm Bioallied Sci. 2011;3(1):118-127.
references.usedFor: Negative APPs: albumin, transferrin, transthyretin, transcortin, retinol-binding protein; positive APPs include CRP, AAT, α2-macroglobulin, fibrinogen, complement, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, haptoglobin; haptoglobin decreased in hemolytic anemia.

references.citation: Sproston NR, Ashworth JJ. Role of C-reactive protein at sites of inflammation and infection. Front Immunol. 2018;9:754.
references.usedFor: CRP up to 1000-fold in some bacterial infections; falls exponentially over 18–20 h (close to its half-life) after the stimulus ends; IL-6 main inducer.

references.citation: Abboud RT, Nelson TN, Jung B, Mattman A. Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency: a clinical-genetic overview. Appl Clin Genet. 2011;4:55-65.
references.usedFor: Discovery via absent α1-globulin peaks on SPEP; ZZ ≈ 15% of normal; emphysema in smokers at a young age from unopposed neutrophil elastase; Z protein polymerizes and is retained in hepatocytes (neonatal hepatitis, childhood and adult liver disease); quantified by immunoassay, phenotyped by isoelectric focusing, genotyped by DNA analysis.

references.citation: Barcellini W, Fattizzo B. Clinical applications of hemolytic markers in the differential diagnosis and management of hemolytic anemia. Dis Markers. 2015;2015:635670.
references.usedFor: Hemolysis markers (reticulocytes, LD, low haptoglobin, unconjugated bilirubin); haptoglobin is an α2 glycoprotein that binds free hemoglobin; reduced also in liver impairment, malnutrition, congenital hypohaptoglobinemia; increased in inflammation, smokers and nephrotic syndrome, masking hemolysis; hemosiderinuria in marked intravascular hemolysis.

references.citation: Smith A, McCulloh RJ. Hemopexin and haptoglobin: allies against heme toxicity from hemoglobin not contenders. Front Physiol. 2015;6:187.
references.usedFor: Hemopexin binds heme and is not an acute-phase protein in humans, unlike haptoglobin; plasma haptoglobin depleted at high plasma hemoglobin; methemalbumin at high plasma heme.

references.citation: Kapatia G, Wadhwa M, Malhotra P, Prakash G, Aggarwal R. Bisalbuminemia: a pathologist’s insight of an uncommon phenomenon. J Lab Physicians. 2021;13(3):219-223.
references.usedFor: Bisalbuminemia acquired or inherited; hereditary is permanent with rare morbidity; acquired is transient with faster anodal mobility; causes include high-dose penicillin/β-lactams and pancreatic pseudocyst; overtly benign; 0.01% incidence in their cohort.

references.citation: Chhabra S, Bansal F, Saikia B, Minz RW. Bisalbuminemia: a rarely encountered protein anomaly. J Lab Physicians. 2013;5(2):145-146.
references.usedFor: Incidental “slow” variant bisalbuminemia cases (two albumin bands, the variant slower).

references.citation: Petejova N, Martinek A. Acute kidney injury due to rhabdomyolysis and renal replacement therapy: a critical review. Crit Care. 2014;18(3):224.
references.usedFor: Urine: myoglobin or positive dipstick without erythrocytes; serum myoglobin normally bound to plasma globulins such as haptoglobin and α2-globulin.

references.citation: Gupta A, Thorson P, Penmatsa KR, Gupta P. Rhabdomyolysis: revisited. Ulster Med J. 2021;90(2):61-69.
references.usedFor: Dipstick (orthotolidine) detects myoglobin and hemoglobin alike, limiting specificity; excess myoglobin overwhelms binding proteins (mainly haptoglobin); CK as the diagnostic marker.

claims.text: Zone contents; positive APPs (CRP, AAT, Hp, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin, complement) rise and negative APPs (albumin, transferrin, transthyretin) fall in inflammation.
CRP up to ~1000-fold; falls with a ~18–20 h half-life after the stimulus ends.
Absent/faint α1 band in AAT deficiency; ZZ ≈ 15% of normal; early emphysema in smokers; liver injury from retained Z protein; immunoassay, phenotype and genotype.
Nephrotic: albumin ↓, α2 ↑; cirrhosis: albumin ↓, polyclonal γ ↑; iron deficiency: β ↑; inflammation: α1, α2 ↑, albumin ↓.

Heme+ dipstick without RBCs = free Hb or myoglobin; hemolysis lowers Hp and raises LD; hemosiderinuria in marked intravascular hemolysis; CK marks rhabdomyolysis; Hp raised by inflammation, smoking, nephrotic syndrome and lowered by liver disease, malnutrition, congenital; hemopexin not acute-phase.
Hereditary bisalbuminemia permanent and benign; acquired transient (high-dose β-lactams, pancreatic pseudocyst).

α2-macroglobulin 725 kDa rising 10-fold; δ-bilirubin speeds albumin; very high CRP favors bacterial infection; haptoglobin rebounds quickly and hemopexin stays low longer; ZZ 1 in 4000; myoglobin does not bind haptoglobin.
claims.note: Not taught. Not found in the sources read; the myoglobin–haptoglobin statement conflicts with two reviews (rv-myoglobin-hp).

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 4 and its memory hook say myoglobin does not bind haptoglobin; Petejova & Martinek 2014 and Gupta 2021 say circulating myoglobin is bound mainly by haptoglobin. The lesson separates the pigments by haptoglobin/LD vs CK without the binding claim.
Trap 2 calls bisalbuminemia a benign heterozygous variant needing no work-up; Kapatia 2021 also describes a transient acquired form (high-dose β-lactams, pancreatic pseudocyst) with a faster band.
